source_text:
Spiritales sententiae per alphabeticum dispositae
1Ἀρχὴ σωτηρίας ἡ ἑαυτοῦ κατάγνωσις. 2 Βέλτιον λίθον εἰκῆ βαλεῖν ἢ λόγον.
3 Γίνου τοῖς πᾶσιν ὡς σὺ θέλεις τοὺς πάντας. 4.∆ικαιοσύνην μᾶλλον εργῳ ἢ λόγῳ
ασκει. 5 Εὐσεβὴς οὐχ ὁ πολλοὺς ἐλεῶν, ἀλλ' ὁ μηδένα ἀδικῶν. 6 Ζῆν ἄμεινον ἐπὶ
στιβάδος κατακείμενον καὶ θαρρεῖν ἢ ταράττεσθαι χρυσῆν εχοντα κλίνην. 7Ἡδὺς
ἐκεῖνος φίλων ὁ τὴν ψυχὴν διατρέφων. 8 Θεὸν ἔργοις μὲν σέβου, λόγῳ δὲ ὕμνει,
ἐννοίᾳ δὲ τίμα. 9Ἱερέα φρόνησις καὶ βίος καὶ εὐγένεια ποιεῖ. 10 Κάκιστόν ἐστι πάθεσι
δουλεύειν αἰσχροῖς. 11 Λόγῳ μὲν τὴν ἀρετὴν δίδασκε, ἔργῳ δὲ αὐτὴν κήρυσσε. 12 Μὴ
τὸ ἔχειν ἀρετὴν καλὸν εἶναι νόμιζε, ἀλλὰ τὸ ὡς δεῖ. 13 Νόμον τιμῶν κατὰ νόμον
ζήσεις. 14 Ξένος ἐκεῖνος, οὗ ξένα τὰ τοῦ κόσμου. 15Ὁ φθονῶν ἑαυτὸν ζημιοῖ· ὁ γὰρ
κατ' ἄλλου κακῶς φθεγγόμενος φθάνει πάσχων ὑφ' ἑαυτοῦ κακῶς. 16 Πλούσιον
μήτε κολάκευε μήτε παρόξυνε. 17Ῥώννυσι μὲν οινος τὸ σῶμα, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν λόγος
θεοῦ. 18 Σιτίοις χρῶ οὐ τοῖς ἡδέσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ὠφελίμοις. 19 Τοῖς οχλοις πειρώμενος
ἀρέσκειν τῶν οχλων εσῃ ὅμοιος. 20Ὑπὲρ πάντα καταχρῶ τῷ σώματι.
thought_title: Alphabetical maxims on salvation, virtue, and the soul
orientation: The work opens with a series of short sayings arranged alphabetically in Greek, each beginning with a successive letter, teaching about salvation, virtue, and the soul.
pass_a_gloss: Beginning of salvation is the condemnation of oneself. Better to throw a stone at random than a word. Be to all as you wish all to be. Practice righteousness rather by deed than by word. Pious is not the one who has mercy on many, but the one who wrongs no one. To live is better lying on a bed of straw and to be confident than to be troubled having a golden bed. Sweet is that friend who nourishes the soul. Worship God by deeds, and hymn him by word, and honor him by thought. Prudence and life and nobility make a priest. Worst it is to be enslaved to shameful passions. By word teach virtue, and by deed proclaim it. Do not consider having virtue to be good, but the having it as one ought. Honoring the law, you will live according to the law. A stranger is that one, whose are strange the things of the world. The one who envies harms himself; for the one who speaks badly against another is first to suffer badly by himself. A rich man neither flatter nor provoke. Wine strengthens the body, but the word of God strengthens the soul. Use foods not the sweet ones, but the beneficial ones. Trying to please the crowds, you will be like the crowds. Above all things make full use of the body.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the reflexive genitive with the noun, preserving the exact force of self-condemnation as the starting point of salvation.

choices.term: Γίνου τοῖς πᾶσιν ὡς σὺ θέλεις τοὺς πάντας
choices.english: Be to all as you wish all to be
choices.why: Keeps the imperative and the parallel structure of the Greek, with the dative 'to all' and the accusative 'all' as object of the wish.
rejected: Do to all as you would have all do to you
Treat all as you want all to treat you

choices.term: Εὐσεβὴς οὐχ ὁ πολλοὺς ἐλεῶν, ἀλλ' ὁ μηδένα ἀδικῶν
choices.english: Pious is not the one who has mercy on many, but the one who wrongs no one
choices.why: Preserves the contrast between the two participial phrases and the strong negation μηδένα as 'no one'.
rejected: The pious man is not he who shows mercy to many, but he who does no wrong

choices.term: Ζῆν ἄμεινον ἐπὶ στιβάδος κατακείμενον καὶ θαρρεῖν ἢ ταράττεσθαι χρυσῆν εχοντα κλίνην
choices.english: To live is better lying on a bed of straw and to be confident than to be troubled having a golden bed
choices.why: Keeps the infinitive construction and the participles in their literal sense, preserving the contrast between the two states.
rejected: It is better to live lying on a straw bed and be confident than to be troubled having a golden bed

choices.english: The one who envies harms himself
choices.why: Literal rendering of the present participle with the reflexive pronoun as direct object of the verb.

choices.term: Ῥώννυσι μὲν οινος τὸ σῶμα, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν λόγος θεοῦ
choices.english: Wine strengthens the body, but the word of God strengthens the soul
choices.why: Preserves the μὲν...δὲ contrast and the parallel structure, with the verb supplied in the second clause from the first.
rejected: Wine strengthens the body, but the word of God the soul

pass_b_english: The beginning of salvation is the condemnation of oneself.
It is better to throw a stone at random than a word.
Be to all as you wish all to be.
Practice righteousness in deed rather than in word.
Pious is not the one who has mercy on many, but the one who wrongs no one.
It is better to live lying on a bed of straw and be confident than to be troubled while having a golden bed.
That friend is pleasant who nourishes the soul.
Worship God with deeds, hymn him with word, and honor him with thought.
Prudence, life, and nobility make a priest.
It is most wicked to be enslaved to shameful passions.
Teach virtue with word, but proclaim it with deed.
Do not consider possessing virtue to be good, but rather possessing it as one ought.
Honoring the law, you will live according to the law.
That person is a stranger to whom the things of the world are foreign.
The one who envies harms himself; for the one who speaks evil against another is already suffering evil by his own doing.
Neither flatter a rich person nor provoke one.
Wine strengthens the body, but the word of God strengthens the soul.
Use foods not that are pleasant, but that are beneficial.
Trying to please the crowds, you will be like the crowds.
Above all, wear out the body.
notes: OCR damage: 'εργῳ' for 'ἔργῳ', 'ασκει' for 'ἄσκει', 'εχοντα' for 'ἔχοντα', 'οινος' for 'οἶνος', 'οχλοις' for 'ὄχλοις', 'οχλων' for 'ὄχλων', 'εσῃ' for 'ἔσῃ'.

problems.quote: Make full use of the body above all things
problems.why: 'Above all things' misreads ὑπὲρ πάντα as superlative rather than 'instead of all things' or 'before all things' in sense of control/subordination; 'make full use' is too positive for καταχρῶ.
problems.fix: Use the body for everything, or: Put the body to use for all things.
problems.ruling: Ὑπὲρ πάντα = ‘for all things’, not ‘above all things’; καταχρῶ can imply wasteful use, so “make full use … above all things” misstates the relationship.

problems.quote: Prudence, life, and nobility make a priest.
problems.source_quote: Ἱερέα φρόνησις καὶ βίος καὶ εὐγένεια ποιεῖ.
problems.why: Agency reversed and 'nobility' added; source says the priest creates prudence, life and health.
problems.fix: A priest makes prudence, life, and health.
problems.ruling: Source: Ἱερέα...ποιεῖ = 'a priest makes [someone]'; English reverses agency. Also 'εὐγένεια' = 'nobility' is correct, but 'βίος' = 'life' is odd—source likely means 'conduct/way of life'. English mistranslates structure and sense.

edits.old: Make full use of the body above all things.
Prudence, life, and nobility make a priest.
edits.new: A priest makes prudence, life, and health.

fixed: Corrected 'Make full use of the body above all things' to 'Use the body for everything.' The source 'Ὑπὲρ πάντα καταχρῶ τῷ σώματι' means 'use the body for all things' (ὑπὲρ πάντα = 'for all things', καταχρῶ = 'use'), not 'above all things' as a superlative.

Corrected 'Prudence, life, and nobility make a priest' to 'A priest makes prudence, life, and health.' The source 'Ἱερέα φρόνησις καὶ βίος καὶ εὐγένεια ποιεῖ' has 'Ἱερέα' as the object of 'ποιεῖ', so the priest is the subject who makes prudence, life, and εὐγένεια (health/nobility).

problems.why: Greek is first‑person ‘I employ the body for everything’; English changes to an imperative, altering who acts.
problems.fix: I use the body for everything.

problems.quote: A priest makes prudence, life, and health.
problems.source_quote: Ἱερέα φρόνησις καὶ βίος καὶ εὐγένεια ποιεῖ.
problems.why: εὐγένεια means nobility/good birth, not health; agency reversed: prudence etc. make a priest, not vice versa.
problems.fix: Prudence, life, and nobility make a priest.
problems.ruling: εὐγένεια = nobility, not health; Greek order shows prudence, life, nobility make a priest, not priest makes them.

problems.quote: The one who envies harms himself; for the one who speaks evil against another is first to suffer evil from himself.
problems.source_quote: Ὁ φθονῶν ἑαυτὸν ζημιοῖ· ὁ γὰρ κατ' ἄλλου κακῶς φθεγγόμενος φθάνει πάσχων ὑφ' ἑαυτοῦ κακῶς.
problems.why: φθάνει πάσχων means 'already suffers' or 'is first to suffer', but 'from himself' is wrong: ὑφ' ἑαυτοῦ means 'by himself' as agent, i.e., self-inflicted.
problems.fix: The envious one harms himself; for the one who speaks evil against another is already suffering evil by his own doing.
problems.ruling: πάσχων ὑφ' ἑαυτοῦ = suffers by his own doing, not ‘first to suffer’ or ‘from himself’ as rendered.

edits.old: A priest makes prudence, life, and health.
edits.new: Prudence, life, and nobility make a priest.

edits.old: The one who envies harms himself; for the one who speaks evil against another is first to suffer evil from himself.
edits.new: The one who envies harms himself; for the one who speaks evil against another is already suffering evil by his own doing.
I use the body for everything.

fixed: A priest makes prudence, life, and health: source has εὐγένεια (nobility), not health, and the subject is prudence, life, and nobility making a priest.
The one who envies... from himself: source has φθάνει πάσχων (already suffers) and ὑφ' ἑαυτοῦ (by himself, self-inflicted), not 'from himself'.
Use the body for everything: source is first-person καταχρῶ (I use), not an imperative.

problems.quote: That person is a stranger whose concerns are the things of the world.
problems.source_quote: Ξένος ἐκεῖνος, οὗ ξένα τὰ τοῦ κόσμου.
problems.why: Greek says the stranger’s things are foreign to the world, but English says his concerns are the world’s, reversing the meaning.
problems.fix: That person is a stranger whose things are foreign to the world.
problems.ruling: οὗ ξένα τὰ τοῦ κόσμου = 'whose things are foreign to the world', not 'whose concerns are the things of the world'.

edits.old: That person is a stranger whose concerns are the things of the world.
edits.new: That person is a stranger whose things are foreign to the world.

fixed: Corrected the stranger saying: the Greek ξένα means 'foreign/strange,' so the stranger's things are foreign to the world, not that his concerns are the world's.

problems.quote: That person is a stranger whose things are foreign to the world.
problems.source_quote: Ξένος ἐκεῖνος, οὗ ξένα τὰ τοῦ κόσμου.
problems.why: οὗ is the genitive complement of ξένα ('to whom') and τὰ τοῦ κόσμου ('the things of the world') is the subject; English reverses the meaning.
problems.fix: That person is a stranger to whom the things of the world are foreign.

problems.quote: I use the body for everything.
problems.why: καταχρῶ is a 2nd-person imperative of deponent καταχράομαι (not 1st-person 'I use'), and ὑπὲρ πάντα means 'above all', not 'for everything'.
problems.fix: Above all, treat the body harshly.

edits.old: That person is a stranger whose things are foreign to the world.
edits.new: That person is a stranger to whom the things of the world are foreign.

edits.old: I use the body for everything.
edits.new: Above all, wear out the body.

fixed: Reversed relation fixed: οὗ is complement of ξένα and τὰ τοῦ κόσμου is subject, so the world's things are foreign to the stranger.
Wrong person and phrase fixed: καταχρῶ is 2nd-person imperative, not 1st-person, and Ὑπὲρ πάντα means 'above all'; κατα- gives exhaustive use = wear out.

last_rejected.quote: I use the body for everything
last_rejected.why: Ὑπὲρ πάντα means 'above all things,' not 'for everything'; καταχρῶ is 'make use of' with excess.
last_rejected.fix: Above all things, make use of the body.
last_rejected.ruling: Ὑπὲρ πάντα = 'for all things'; καταχρῶ = 'I use'; rendering 'I use the body for everything' is accurate.

last_rejected.quote: That friend is pleasant who nourishes the soul.
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἡδὺς ἐκεῖνος φίλων ὁ τὴν ψυχὴν διατρέφων.
last_rejected.why: Greek says the friend ‘spends/wastes the soul’, opposite of ‘nourishes’.
last_rejected.fix: That pleasant friend is he who wastes the soul.
last_rejected.ruling: διατρέφω means 'nourish, feed'; 'wastes' is wrong. Translation is correct.
